content.title: About
content.content: Refrigerated dough biscuit is a ready‑to‑bake product made from specially prepared dough that is kept chilled until use. The dough contains flour, eggs, sugar, butter and leavening agents, and may include flavorings and additives. After baking, the biscuit is light, airy and tender.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chilled dough stays fresh longer than regular dough.
Refrigerated dough biscuits are widely used in professional bakeries to speed up cake and dessert production.
The dough can be pre‑shaped into rounds, squares or rectangles for easy portioning.
Biscuit layers are often paired with creams, berries and fruit fillings.
When stored properly in the fridge, the dough retains its quality for up to 7 days.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The biscuit provides carbohydrates that quickly supply the body with energy.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Eggs in the dough contribute a modest amount of animal protein.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dough supplies B1, B2 and B6 vitamins, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It contains calcium and iron, important for bones and blood.

items.title: Convenient preparation
items.content: The ready‑made product saves time, allowing fresh biscuits to be baked without mixing dough from scratch.

items.title: Egg and dairy allergy
items.content: The dough contains eggs and butter, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Biscuit may be sweet, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Trans‑fat content
items.content: If partially hydrogenated oil is used, trans fats may be present.

items.title: Shelf life
items.content: After opening, keep the dough refrigerated and use within a few days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bake the refrigerated dough biscuit at 180 °C for 12–15 minutes, then use it as a base for cakes, desserts, pancakes, or serve with fruit sauce, berries and whipped cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the package in the refrigerator at 2–6 °C. Once opened, consume within 5–7 days. For longer storage, freeze the dough at –18 °C, but allow it to thaw completely before baking.

burrito-beef-with-rice-cheese.title: Beef Burrito with Rice and Cheese

content.title: About
content.content: The beef burrito with rice and cheese is a Mexican dish consisting of a large soft tortilla filled with sautéed beef, cooked rice, shredded cheese, and often additional ingredients such as beans, salsa, and sour cream. The combination delivers a hearty, savory flavor with the creaminess of cheese and the comforting texture of rice.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Burritos originated in northern Mexico, where tortillas served as a portable “container” for meals.
Beef in burritos is often prepared as carne asada—marinated and quickly grilled for a smoky flavor.
Mexican rice used in burritos is typically cooked with tomato sauce and spices, giving it a distinctive red hue.
Cheese commonly added is cheddar or Mexican “queso” that melts smoothly and binds the filling.
The hand‑held nature of burritos made them a staple of street vendors and fast‑food menus worldwide.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Beef provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Energy‑rich carbohydrates
items.content: Rice supplies complex carbs that offer sustained energy and satiety.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus
items.content: Cheese contributes calcium and phosphorus, important for bone health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both beef and rice contain B‑vitamins (B12, B6, niacin) that support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Beef is a good source of heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: A beef, rice, and cheese burrito can be calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Cheese and beef contain saturated fats that may affect cholesterol levels if consumed in excess.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Cheese and prepared sauces often add significant sodium; individuals with hypertension should choose lower‑salt options.

items.title: Dairy allergy or lactose intolerance
items.content: People with dairy sensitivities should replace cheese with suitable alternatives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Burritos are designed to be handheld; warm them in a microwave or on a skillet until the tortilla is lightly crisp. Add fresh toppings such as lettuce, salsa, guacamole, or sour cream for extra flavor and texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared burrito in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. For longer keeping, freeze in a freezer‑safe bag for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Crab cake is a dish made from crab meat, breadcrumbs, eggs, and seasonings. The cakes are usually pan‑fried until golden, offering a tender, slightly sweet seafood flavor combined with aromatic herbs and spices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Crab cakes are especially popular in coastal regions of the United States, notably Maryland and Virginia.
The classic recipe includes crab meat, mayonnaise, mustard, Worcestershire sauce, and lemon juice.
Crab meat is high in protein and low in fat, making crab cakes a relatively light option.
Traditional recipes use only crab meat, without added fish or other seafood.
Crab cakes are often served with tartar sauce or a lemon‑butter drizzle.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Crab meat provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with many meat patties, crab cakes contain little saturated fat.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: Crab is a good source of zinc, selenium, and copper, which support immune function and antioxidant defenses.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Crab meat supplies vitamin B12 and B6, important for nervous system health and metabolism.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Crab provides modest amounts of omega‑3s that contribute to heart health.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to crab, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared crab cakes often contain added salt and sauces, increasing sodium levels.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: Crabs can accumulate toxins and heavy metals; it is important to source them from reputable suppliers.

items.title: Increased calories when fried
items.content: Pan‑frying adds oil, raising the calorie count and fat content of the final dish.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Crab cakes can be served hot as a main course, in burgers, with salads, or as an appetizer. They are commonly accompanied by tartar sauce, lemon mayo, or a spicy chili sauce. Baking the cakes in the oven reduces added fat while still delivering a crisp exterior.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh crab meat should be kept in the refrigerator for no more than 2 days. Cooked crab cakes store in an airtight container in the fridge for 3‑4 days or can be frozen for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Wheat Thins are thin, crunchy wheat crackers flavored with a light seasoning. They have a subtle nutty taste with a hint of salt and are commonly enjoyed as a snack or paired with cheese and dips.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wheat Thins were first introduced in the United States in 1947 as part of Nabisco's product line.
They were originally developed as a healthier alternative to traditional crackers by using whole wheat.
The recipe often includes vegetable oil, but some versions use olive oil for a milder flavor.
Crackers are frequently used in recipes, such as mini‑pizzas or as a breadcrumb substitute.
Various flavored versions (spice, cheese, sweet) are sold worldwide under the Wheat Thins brand.

items.title: Source of whole grains
items.content: Made from whole wheat, they provide dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Most varieties contain minimal added sugar, making them suitable for moderate consumption.

items.title: Contains iron and B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat supplies iron, thiamine, and niacin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: Fiber and a modest amount of protein help keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Low in trans fats
items.content: Modern formulations typically exclude trans fats, benefiting heart health.

items.title: Wheat and gluten allergy
items.content: The product contains gluten and is not suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some varieties can be relatively salty; choose low‑sodium options if you monitor salt intake.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: While light, the crackers can add up in calories if eaten in large amounts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy them straight from the bag, pair with cheese, hummus, guacamole, or use in recipes—as a base for mini‑pizzas, in salads, or as a breadcrumb alternative.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in the original packaging or an airtight container. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator to maintain crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Infant formula enriched with a complex of amino acids is designed for complete nutrition of babies from birth to 12 months. The formula provides essential proteins, vitamins, and minerals to support growth and development.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Amino acids are often supplied in free form, making them easier for infants to absorb.
The formula may be fortified with DHA and ARA, fatty acids important for brain and eye development.
Some brands use hydrolyzed milk proteins to reduce the risk of allergy.
The product undergoes strict quality control and meets international infant nutrition standards.
Prebiotics may be added to support a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Supports tissue growth
items.content: Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins needed for muscle, organ, and immune system development.

items.title: Enhances brain development
items.content: DHA and ARA in the formula aid cognitive function and visual system maturation.

items.title: Reduces allergy risk
items.content: Hydrolyzed proteins are less allergenic, benefiting infants with a predisposition to food allergies.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Prebiotics and easily digestible amino acids promote a healthy intestinal flora.

items.title: Provides energy
items.content: Amino acids are quickly converted into energy, sustaining the active growth of the baby.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some infants may react to milk components even when hydrolyzed.

items.title: Improper dilution
items.content: An overly concentrated solution can strain an infant's kidneys; follow manufacturer instructions.

items.title: Contamination from poor storage
items.content: Open packaging can allow bacterial growth, so store according to guidelines.

items.title: Overconsumption
items.content: Excessive formula intake may lead to rapid weight gain; adhere to age‑appropriate feeding volumes.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Prepare the formula by mixing the specified amount of powder with boiled, cooled water to body temperature. Feed using a sterilized bottle, maintaining hygiene and following recommended portion sizes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the container in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. After opening, use within 30 days and keep tightly sealed. Do not store prepared formula at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Gerber NFS is an infant formula designed for newborns and babies, meeting the requirements of the U.S. National Formulation Standard (NFS). It contains carefully selected proteins, fats, carbohydrates, vitamins, and minerals essential for growth and development during the first months of life.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Gerber is one of the oldest infant‑nutrition brands, founded in 1851.
The NFS formula is developed according to the recommendations of the American Academy of Pediatrics.
The product undergoes strict quality control and certification to international standards.
It includes DHA and ARA – fatty acids important for brain and eye development.
The packaging protects the powder from moisture and light, preserving its nutritional value.

items.title: Supports growth
items.content: A balanced ratio of protein, fat, and carbohydrate provides energy and building blocks for tissue development.

items.title: Brain development
items.content: DHA and ARA help form neural cells and support visual system maturation.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamins A, C, D and zinc contribute to the body’s defense mechanisms.

items.title: Bone health
items.content: Calcium and phosphorus in optimal proportions promote bone mineralization.

items.title: Easy digestion
items.content: Hydrolyzed proteins and prebiotics aid comfortable digestion in newborns.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some infants may develop an allergy to cow’s milk; consult a pediatrician at the first signs.

items.title: Incorrect reconstitution
items.content: Follow the exact water‑to‑powder ratio to avoid hypo‑ or hyper‑osmolar solutions.

items.title: Storage after preparation
items.content: Prepared formula should be used within 48 hours; otherwise bacterial growth risk increases.

items.title: Temperature control
items.content: Do not heat the formula in a microwave to prevent hot spots that could burn the baby.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Mix the specified amount of powder with clean, boiled water cooled to room temperature. Feed according to pediatrician recommendations, typically 6‑8 times per day during the first weeks of life.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened containers in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the product in its original sealed container and use within 30 days.

pasta-whole-grain-with-cream-sauce-and-p.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Cream Sauce and Poultry

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain pasta with a creamy sauce and pieces of poultry is a dish made from whole‑grain pasta, a smooth cream‑based sauce, and cooked chicken or turkey. Whole grain pasta retains the bran and germ, providing more nutrients than refined white pasta.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole grain pasta contains more fiber, B‑vitamins, and minerals than traditional refined pasta.
The cream sauce is usually prepared from cream, butter, and a little flour, giving the dish a velvety texture.
Poultry used in the dish is typically chicken or turkey, which are lean sources of high‑quality protein.
The combination of whole grain, cream, and protein makes the meal well‑balanced in macronutrients.
In Italy, whole‑grain pasta is called "pasta integrale" and is often served with light sauces, but a creamy sauce with poultry is a popular modern variation.

items.title: High in Fiber
items.content: Whole grain pasta provides both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting digestive health.

items.title: Good Source of Protein
items.content: Poultry adds complete protein essential for muscle maintenance and repair.

items.title: B‑Vitamin Complex
items.content: Whole grains and poultry supply thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Calcium and Vitamin D
items.content: The cream sauce contributes calcium and, when fortified, vitamin D, which are beneficial for bone health.

items.title: Healthy Fats
items.content: Cream contains monounsaturated fats that can support cardiovascular health when consumed in moderation.

items.title: High Calorie Content
items.content: The cream sauce and whole grain pasta make the dish energy‑dense; portion control is advised, especially on weight‑loss diets.

items.title: Lactose Intolerance
items.content: Cream may cause discomfort for those who are lactose intolerant; lactose‑free or plant‑based alternatives can be used.

items.title: Poultry Allergy
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to chicken or turkey and should avoid the dish.

items.title: Sodium Levels
items.content: If the sauce is seasoned with salt, the meal can be high in sodium; use salt sparingly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta hot, tossed with the creamy sauce and poultry pieces. Garnish with fresh herbs such as parsley or basil and a sprinkle of grated Parmesan. For a dairy‑free version, replace the cream with a plant‑based alternative.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. The cream sauce may separate; gently reheat and stir before serving. Keep dry whole‑grain pasta in a cool, dry place.

content.title: About
content.content: Taco or Tostada Salad, meatless is a light dish inspired by Mexican cuisine. It features crisp leafy greens, corn, beans, avocado, tomatoes and aromatic spices, served with a yogurt‑based or salsa dressing. The product is fully plant‑based with no meat added.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional Mexican tacos are usually made with beef, but vegetarian versions use beans, tofu or soy crumble.
A tostada is a crunchy corn flatbread topped with a taco‑style filling.
Avocado provides a creamy texture and heart‑healthy monounsaturated fats.
The beans used in the salad are an excellent source of plant protein and fiber.
The salad is often finished with lime, which brightens flavor and adds vitamin C.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Beans and tofu supply a complete set of amino acids, supporting muscle maintenance and overall health.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Avocado and olive‑oil‑based dressing provide monounsaturated fats beneficial for heart health.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Corn, beans and vegetables aid digestion and promote satiety.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The salad is a good source of vitamin C, vitamin K, folate and potassium, which support immunity and metabolism.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Absence of meat and use of plant ingredients make the dish suitable for low‑saturated‑fat diets.

items.title: Bean or soy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans, soy crumble or tofu.

items.title: High sodium in sauces
items.content: Prepared salsas or dressings can be salty; choose low‑sodium versions when possible.

items.title: Lime acidity
items.content: Large amounts of lime juice may irritate the stomach in people with acid reflux.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled, optionally topped with fresh salsa, guacamole or a yogurt dressing. It pairs well with tortillas, corn chips, or can be enjoyed as a standalone bowl.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Stir before serving to evenly distribute the dressing.

content.title: About
content.content: Venison jerky is dried deer meat that is seasoned with a modest amount of salt, spices, and sometimes sugar. The meat is sliced into thin strips and slowly dried at low temperature, preserving most nutrients while giving it a distinctive savory flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Venison is a leaner meat than beef, containing very little fat.
Traditional drying of meat was a common preservation method in northern regions before refrigeration.
Jerky is often flavored with natural herbs such as rosemary, black pepper, garlic, and maple syrup.
Deer meat is rich in heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.
Venison jerky is popular among hunters and travelers as a lightweight, protein‑dense snack.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Venison provides about 30 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many other meats, venison jerky contains less than 5 g of fat per 100 g, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Rich source of iron
items.content: The heme iron in venison helps prevent anemia and supports oxygen transport.

items.title: Contains zinc and vitamin B12
items.content: These micronutrients aid immune function and nervous system health.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Jerky has minimal impact on blood sugar, which is beneficial for people with diabetes.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to deer meat proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Salt is often added for preservation; those monitoring sodium intake should choose low‑salt versions.

items.title: Quality of raw material
items.content: Poor‑quality meat can harbor parasites or bacteria; purchase from reputable sources.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some jerky products contain nitrites or other additives; check labels if you are sensitive.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Venison jerky can be eaten straight from the package, added to salads, soups, or used in noodle dishes. For a softer texture, briefly warm it in the microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep jerky in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For extended storage, refrigerate or freeze to prevent fat oxidation. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.
